newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japanese management under fire after scandals.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japanese management under fire after scandals.

text.p: An epidemic of scandals at top Japanese firms is fuelling calls to reform management practices that fail to hold executives accountable for their actions.
Optimists say the uproar could prove a catalyst for change, and some reforms are already afoot at major companies.
But efforts to alter a culture that values consensus and "old-boy" personal loyalties while placing a low priority on shareholders' interests will hardly succeed overnight.
Bureaucrats have taken much of the heat in Japan's debate over the need to revamp a system that once spelled economic success but is now seen as in need of far-reaching reform.

But fresh revelations of corporate management misdeeds, including a widening scandal of alleged illegal payoffs and dubious deals with racketeers that has ensnared two giant financial institutions, Nomura Securities and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, have turned up the heat on executive boardroom behaviour.

"There is a possibility of rapid improvement on the part of the private sector and this should be considered simultaneously with bureaucratic reform," said Taichi Sakaiya, a former trade official and now co-chairman of a wise men's group, the U.S.-Japan 21st Century Committee.
"In the past cultural context, personal relations were very strong and power and authority were vaguely defined. We feel this should be reformed," Sakaiya told reporters this week.
CALLS MOUNT TO IMPROVE CORPORATE GOVERNANCE

Calls for improved "corporate governance" -- including more attention to shareholders' interests and the adoption of transparent, accountable management styles -- have grown louder since the bursting of Japan's late 1980s "bubble" economy of soaring asset prices forced firms at least to pay lip service to shareholders' interests.

But the latest round of scandals has highlighted deficiencies in management practices which are viewed not only as short on corporate ethics but also inadequate to ensure success in an increasingly competitive global marketplace.

"In order for companies to compete fairly and boost productivity, it is essential to create a management structure that makes responsibility to shareholders clear, discloses information and has effective checks and balances," said an editorial in the financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun.
"Shouldn't company directors compile and announce a policy on corporate governance, stating how and for whom they exercise their rights, and what checks exist?" the paper said.
MANAGEMENT RESPONSIBILITY REMAINS AMBIGIOUS IN JAPAN
The question of to whom management should be held responsible remains ambiguous in Japan.

"In the Anglo-American world, it's very simple -- the aim is to maximise return to shareholders," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo. "In Japan...a company is in business not just to maximise shareholder value, but to support unions, suppliers and other 'stakeholders'."

That shareholders' interests can get short shrift seemed apparent this week, after a corporate struggle within Bandai Co Ltd which ended in the cancellation of the toymaker's planned merger with video game-maker Sega Enterprises Ltd

On Tuesday, one day after Bandai called a news conference to confirm that the merger would go ahead, the two firms announced separately that the corporate engagement had been broken, due largely to opposition by Bandai middle-managers.
"One cannot feel that there was a sense of responsibility to disclose accurate information to investors," remarked one media report of the failed merger affair.

In a typical display of executive remorse, Bandai President Makoto Yamashina then offered to resign as president -- but take up the post of chairman -- to "take responsibility" for the failed merger scheme.

Such ritual resignations, which often leave executives with lucrative but lower-profile posts, are being greeted with diminishing enthusiasm. "There is a longing for 'decisionism,' in which people actually make decisions and are held accountable for them," Koll said.
JAPANESE DECISION-MAKING OPAQUE AND UNWIELDY

Japanese management is also under attack for the opacity of its decision-making, for an unwieldy structure which slows response to change, and for an absence of checks on executive decisions by outside forces -- either in the form of outside directors, external auditors, or vocal and powerful investors.
The roots of the Nomura scandal appear to lie in part in the "shadow shogun" role retained by former executives Setsuya Tabuchi and Yoshihisa Tabuchi (no relation).

The two men wielded considerable influence over Nomura management even after resigning over a 1991 scandal that included links to gangsters. They returned to the board in 1995, much to the dismay of many of the brokerage's own employees.
"Socially, people tend to be more powerful when they act in the shadows than when they operate in the public eye," said Darrel Whitten, director of research at Lehman Brothers Japan.
CHANGES UNDER WAY AT SOME FIRMS
A few Japanese companies -- unscathed by scandal but seeking to improve corporate accountability and management efficiency -- have begun to implement changes.
Sony Corporation is slashing the number of its board of directors to 10 from 38 to speed up policy formation and will appoint two more outside directors for a total of three.
Other companies are following suit.

Cosmetic maker Shiseido Co Ltd said this week that it planned to abolish its managing directors' meeting and unify decision-making in its board of directors. It aims to cut the number of directors to about 15 from the current 23 over the next two to three years.
Some business leaders see hopes of more improvements ahead.
"We Japanese have developed a sort of...talent to transform negative problems into positive blessings," said Masaya Miyoshi, outgoing director general of the influential business lobby Keidanren.
"The most important thing is discipline and corporate governance -- 100 percent transparency and accountability to shareholders," Miyoshi said.
"This has been somewhat ambiguous in Japanese corporate society, but from now on we will come closer and closer to international society."
